title: Souls Would Ransom You and Never Draw Back
intro: The commentaries on Saqt al-Zand identify the traveller as al-Ma'arri’s maternal uncle, Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Sabika, who had gone west. The family imagine kissing even the necks of his camels when he returns. Across rivers, under the stars and out among Byzantine ships, the poet follows the very journeys he wants his uncle to give up. He closes by leaving him free to refuse.

translation: Souls would ransom you and never draw back.
Come close, or prolong your absence.
1.sharh: Distance makes no difference to the family’s offer of their lives. Al-Batalyawsi also hears a refusal of reciprocity. Someone so dear may be ransomed, but must never give his life for theirs.

translation: I find that we, Ali, though we have stayed behind,
share your longing and your sleepless nights.
2.sharh: The people at home and the traveller each take a share of the same longing. The verb makes sleeplessness sound like something the two households could divide between them.

translation: If we did not fear being thought extravagant,
we would say more to anyone who asked.
3.sharh: He checks himself because a fuller account of their longing might sound exaggerated. The restraint hints at how much still goes unsaid.

translation: “They say he gained wealth by travelling.”
We said, “Did he gain a heart as well?”
4.sharh: People report a profit that can be counted. The family want to know whether travel has taught him to feel their absence, or won him a heart as devoted as theirs.

translation: And have his resolutions softened and given way?
Their grain was hard once.
5.sharh: They hope his determination to keep travelling may have softened. The word for its temper evokes something pressed by hand to see how firmly it holds.

translation: When the stars race you through the night, they say,
“God help whichever of us has further to go.”
6.sharh: Even the stars find themselves in a contest when he travels by night. Their prayer leaves open which competitor has set the more distant goal.

translation: If the wild winds race you, they have
wearier mounts and fewer provisions.
7.sharh: The wind becomes another rider beside him. A gale eventually dies down, as if its mounts tired first and its provisions ran out.

translation: When travelling unveils the month’s nights before you,
you take the one most deeply clad in mourning.
8.sharh: Travel presents the nights like brides unveiled for his choice. He picks the one dressed most fully in a mourner’s black, the very night another traveller would avoid.

translation: You choose the black ones and say, “The loveliest
eyes in all creation are the darkest.”
9.sharh: He gives his preference an unexpected reason. The depth of black admired in an eye becomes the measure of beauty in a night.

translation: In the wastes the limping beasts come as your guests.
You feed them, two together or one at a time.
10.sharh: The desert scavengers seek him out as guests, and he feeds them in whatever number they come. The commentaries hear a traveller so familiar with these empty places that even their wild animals know his company.

translation: Every rain-star weeps for you in tenderness.
From its tears you fill the waterskins.
11.sharh: Each star associated with rain takes pity on him. Its tears supply the very practical need of filling his water bags.

translation: If the crow calls to announce your coming near,
we shall turn its black hair-dye to saffron.
12.sharh: The crow normally foretells separation. If it announces a reunion instead, the family will reward the messenger by exchanging the black of its head for saffron.

translation: We shall steep in perfume one of its wings,
black as if it had been painted with ink.
13.sharh: The reward spreads from the crow’s head to its wing. Imagining the black as a coat of ink makes it possible to picture putting another colour and scent over it.

translation: We shall kiss the necks of your fine camels
and press our lips to sword sheath and baldric.
14.sharh: The welcome reaches the camels that carried him and the sword fittings that touched him. Sipping is the verb used for the long kiss they would give even his scabbard.

translation: We shall seek a cure in what your fine horse leaves
after you come riding in, if thirst threatens us.
15.sharh: They would drink the water left by the horse that brought him home. Horse and thirst have almost identical names here, distinguished by a single vowel.

translation: On its back you seem above a heaven of honour,
its legs set there as pillars.
16.sharh: The horse’s back changes into a sky of honour under its rider. Once the horse is seen that way, its four legs become the pillars holding that sky up.

translation: If one of us gave his brother
your dust, it would be the choicest gift.
17.sharh: Dust gains its value solely from contact with the traveller. The family imagine passing it from hand to hand as their most thoughtful present.

translation: The sons of Sabika might be riding birds,
so swiftly they cross the hollows and the heights.
18.sharh: The address opens out from Ali to his whole family. Their progress across uneven ground looks as effortless as flying straight over it.

translation: Is King Alexander the man you took for your example,
that you never lay a pillow down in any land?
19.sharh: Alexander’s travels across the known world supply a grand precedent. A pillow that never gets laid down brings the comparison back to the ordinary business of finding somewhere to sleep.

translation: Perhaps, stout-hearted man, you come second
to the first surveyor who measured out the lands.
20.sharh: He has covered the earth as thoroughly as someone measuring it. Al-Tabrizi takes the first surveyor to be the Alexander just mentioned. Al-Khwarazmi also records an identification with Jesus.

translation: With pale camels like the teeth of combs
that wade through the tightly curled locks of darkness.
21.sharh: The lean camels become comb teeth. Once darkness takes the form of black curls, the reader can see the caravan passing through it as a comb through tangled hair.

translation: Why did you leave the east behind
and come west to test its people?
22.sharh: The family try to imagine a purpose large enough to explain the distance. Perhaps, they suggest with some reproach, he has gone to find out what everyone in the west is like.

translation: For a time Egypt with its Nile
contended for you with the Tigris and the Sawad.
23.sharh: Egypt and the cultivated lands of Iraq become rival hosts. The rivers recall two regions he already knew before he went further west.

translation: From the Sarat to the course of the Euphrates,
and on to the Quwayq, there is room enough to roam.
24.sharh: The route from Baghdad’s canal to Aleppo’s river offers ample scope for someone who loves to range about. In Arabic the metrical division falls inside the name of the Euphrates.

translation: Waters where, if you threw in silver
and its lookalike, the silver could be told apart by assay.
25.sharh: The water is so clear that even through it a piece of silver could be distinguished from a lookalike. The passive verb leaves the assayer unnamed. Another reading of the image makes the clear water itself resemble silver.

translation: Even if you find the country to a stranger’s liking,
his friend has not got what he wanted.
26.sharh: The same place can satisfy the traveller and disappoint the friend who waits at home. The two wishes are heard against one another across the halves.

translation: When the Yemeni Dog Star shines,
renew your affection for its Syrian sister.
27.sharh: Sirius and Procyon bear paired Arabic names looking south towards Yemen and north towards Syria. Admiring the one should recall the other, just as a foreign country might bring home to mind.

translation: For Syria has fidelity. Elsewhere
they profess it in words and betray it in their hearts.
28.sharh: Syria stands for its people. The speaker who wants his uncle back weighs the welcome he receives abroad against the lasting attachment of his own people.

translation: You left to win yourself a faithful brother
and let the old one you had won slip away.
29.sharh: The repetition of the verb for acquiring makes the exchange sound particularly poor. He already had precisely what he set out to gain.

translation: You went on to startle the fish, having first
startled the wild beasts and the tawny lions.
30.sharh: Having exhausted the world of land animals, the traveller takes to the sea. The change of creatures lets the reader trace the change in his route.

translation: Many a night, afraid that people would say
it had fled in defeat when it turned away, came back.
31.sharh: A night that seems about to end drags on again. The poet invents a motive for its return, a soldier’s dread of having his retreat called flight.

translation: It grew dark. Mars flared up within it,
and it dressed the ember of the sun in ash.
32.sharh: The darkness intensifies one red light and conceals another. Mars blazes like a new flame while the sun lies buried like an ember under ash.

translation: Among its stars you are like Canopus,
rising apart and all alone.
33.sharh: Canopus appears low and apart from many other bright stars. What makes it the traveller’s likeness is the solitude of its rising.

translation: You enlisted your swift mounts against the night.
Neither you nor they tasted sleep.
34.sharh: He makes the camels his allies in a contest with night. Rider and ridden share the price of their campaign, a night without so much as a taste of sleep.

translation: They fancy that the light of dawn is near,
but their surmise strikes no spark.
35.sharh: It is the mounts that think they see dawn. Their hope fails like an attempt to kindle fire, leaving the source of the glimmer still to be explained.

translation: Morning had not broken for them. They had seen
the fire of your resolve blaze up.
36.sharh: The poet supplies the answer to the camels’ mistake. Their rider is so determined that the heat of his resolve casts a visible glow.

translation: You crossed its seas and its dry land until
you had wrung the last from ships and steeds.
37.sharh: He draws out whatever a first journey has left in his mounts and ships. The verb suggests going back for the last remnant of something apparently used up.

translation: You left no sail to a ship
and no saddle pad to a running mare.
38.sharh: He tells the cost of incessant travel through two pieces of equipment. The sail wears away at sea as the saddle padding wears away on land.

translation: In one land the rain does not fall,
nor do the Bedouin pasture their little sheep there.
39.sharh: Rain and grazing sheep are the measures of a landscape taken from a herder’s world. Al-Batalyawsi identifies the first country as Egypt, with its scant rainfall. Al-Khwarazmi pictures an uninhabited stretch of desert.

translation: In another the Byzantines are Arabs upon it,
though they never ride a horse there.
40.sharh: The Byzantines occupy at sea the position Arab riders hold on open land. Their mastery of movement supplies the resemblance even where a horse cannot be ridden.

translation: Only, there the ships could pass
for haircloth tents in shape and blackness.
41.sharh: The dark coating on the hulls recalls the black haircloth of tents. The ship gives these sailors a portable dwelling as well as a mount.

translation: Their dwellings sail by night and run with them
whenever they choose a raid or a pursuit.
42.sharh: Sea-going raiders take their houses with them. The startling thing about these dwellings is that they can join a pursuit without anybody leaving home.

translation: Their crews hunt in every direction.
The hunter’s end is to be hunted in turn.
43.sharh: There is danger in the change from hunter to quarry, a reversal the commentaries hear in the closing verb. An alternative reading treats the last verb as active, making a catch the hunter’s aim.

translation: In colour and in what they do, their eyes
are all but their sharp spearheads.
44.sharh: The old poetic association of Byzantine eyes with blue-grey steel supplies the colour. A gaze as piercing as a spear supplies the action.

translation: Stay among your kin. Every living thing
receives its livelihood at evening or at morning.
45.sharh: At last he puts the family’s request directly. He names the two daily times at which provisions arrive to suggest that life can be sustained close to home.

translation: Greed brings no one an increase in his portion,
even if he rides the gales to gain it.
46.sharh: A rider on a gale takes the earlier contest with the winds to its utmost. Even that speed could give him no claim to an extra share of livelihood.

translation: How can you travel in search of newly won wealth
when your own fingers gave away your inheritance?
47.sharh: He sets the wealth a man can newly acquire against the property he inherited and has freely given away. The generous uncle makes an unlikely fortune hunter.

translation: A man will always have wealth ready to hand
if he makes contentment his provision.
48.sharh: Contentment becomes a supply he can draw on at any time. The language of equipping a journey now serves someone who could just as easily stay at home.

translation: If clouds gave rain according to reason,
they would not water thornbushes along with the palms.
49.sharh: Clouds let the thirsty thornbush drink beside the fruit-bearing palm. The distribution of rain gives him a visible instance of provision arriving without an assessment of merit.

translation: If it gave by the measure of eminence,
it would water the heights and shun the hollows.
50.sharh: Eminence becomes literal elevation. Rain reaches low ground as surely as a hilltop, just as the earlier cloud reached the thornbush and the palm.

translation: You have always been wise in judgement. Far be it
from one of your gifts to need my reminder.
51.sharh: Having given advice, the nephew acknowledges his uncle’s experience. The difficulty is how to invite a wise man home without appearing to instruct him in wisdom.

translation: A man like you will take the lead of friends.
The worst horse is the hardest to lead.
52.sharh: A good horse answers a light rein. The image lets the nephew make willingness to be guided by friends a mark of good breeding.

translation: Many a man has pressed a matter so hard
that his loved ones tell him, “Take it gently.”
53.sharh: Friends can see when a person’s effort has gone beyond what the task requires. Their intervention gives the family a precedent for speaking now.

translation: Many a hopeful man has seen a matter to its depths
and stopped just when he was close to his goal.
54.sharh: Turning back within reach of an object can be an informed decision. The example gives the uncle a dignified way to reconsider a long pursuit.

translation: We send you our earnest counsel in these rhymes.
It is others we would teach the right course.
55.sharh: Calling the poem a letter returns its many voices to the family who sent it. They can express their wishes without claiming to have better judgement than its recipient.

translation: If you accept, it is what some people long for.
If you refuse, we have spared no effort.
56.sharh: The family who have filled the entire poem become simply “some people” at the close. Their desire has been made plain, and the decision rests with him.

1.1.1.head: فَدّى
1.1.1.meaning: Offers a life or property to ransom another.

1.1.4.meaning: Hold back. One of the two opening syllables is dropped. Another explanation hears the idea of ransoming one another.

1.2.1.head: أَدنِ
1.2.1.meaning: Bring near, here by returning to his family.

2.1.3.head: عَلِيّ
2.1.3.meaning: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Sabika, al-Ma'arri’s maternal uncle and the addressee of the poem.

3.2.5.head: اِستَزادَ
3.2.5.meaning: Asked for more, here for a fuller account of their feelings.

5.2.3.head: عَرائِك
5.2.3.meaning: Its temper or grain, something felt by pressing or rubbing it.

6.1.2.head: سارى
6.1.2.meaning: Travelled by night alongside you, here in rivalry.

6.1.3.head: شُهُب
6.1.3.meaning: Bright stars, here imagined travelling the night sky.

8.1.2.meaning: Displayed or unveiled, as a bride is presented.

8.2.3.head: أَسبَغ
8.2.3.meaning: Fullest or most enveloping, here of a black garment.

10.1.2.head: الخَوامِع
10.1.2.meaning: Limping animals, a name for hyenas, also explained here as including wolves.

10.2.1.head: قَرى
10.2.1.meaning: Set food before them as guests.

11.1.5.head: نَوء
11.1.5.meaning: A star associated with the coming of rain, also the rain of its season.

11.2.4.head: المَزاد
11.2.4.meaning: Leather water bags carried on a journey.

12.1.3-4.head: اِبن دَأيَة
12.1.3-4.meaning: Ibn Da'ya, a name for the crow, whose call was associated with lovers parting.

12.2.3.head: لِمَّة
12.2.3.meaning: Hair hanging near the shoulders, fancifully applied to the crow’s head.

14.1.4.meaning: The camels’ necks, or the mounts that lead the caravan.

14.2.4.head: النِّجاد
14.2.4.meaning: A baldric, the strap on which a sword hangs.

15.1.2.head: سُؤر
15.1.2.meaning: What remains in a vessel after someone has drunk.

15.2.5.head: الجُواد
15.2.5.meaning: Thirst. With a different first vowel the almost identical word in the first half denotes a fine horse.

17.1.2.meaning: Offered a gift, often as part of an exchange.

18.1.2-3.head: بَنو سَبيكَة
18.1.2-3.meaning: Banu Sabika, the family of the poet’s uncle, named for his grandfather.

18.2.2.head: الغَوائِر
18.2.2.meaning: Hollows and low-lying stretches of land.

19.1.1.head: الإِسكَندَر
19.1.1.meaning: Alexander, the king remembered here for travelling east and west.

20.2.2.head: ماسِح
20.2.2.meaning: A land surveyor, here someone who has travelled the length and breadth of the earth.

21.1.1.head: عيس
21.1.1.meaning: Pale camels with a tawny tinge.

21.1.4.meaning: Combs or pointed implements for parting hair.

23.2.3.head: دِجلَة
23.2.3.meaning: Tigris, the river through Baghdad, standing here for Iraq.

23.2.4.head: السَّواد
23.2.4.meaning: Al-Sawad, the irrigated agricultural lands of Iraq.

24.1.3.head: الصَّراة
24.1.3.meaning: Al-Sarat, a Baghdad waterway linking water from the Euphrates to the Tigris.

24.2.3.head: قُوَيق
24.2.3.meaning: Quwayq, the river of Aleppo in northern Syria.

24.2.4.head: مُستَراد
24.2.4.meaning: Room to roam and explore, as a scout seeks pasture.

25.2.1.head: مُشبِه
25.2.1.meaning: An imitation of the silver. The feminine pronoun follows the gender of the ordinary word for silver.

25.2.3.head: اِنتِقاد
25.2.3.meaning: Assaying, the work of telling good coin from counterfeit.

27.1.2-3.head: الشِّعرى اليَمانِيَّة
27.1.2-3.meaning: The Yemeni Dog Star, Sirius, the brighter of the two Dog Stars.

27.2.2.head: الشَّآمِيَّة
27.2.2.meaning: The Syrian Dog Star, Procyon, the northern member of the traditional pair.

28.2.1.meaning: Professed or put on a show of fidelity.

29.1.1.head: ظَعَنَ
29.1.1.meaning: You left home on a journey. The opening consonant is indistinct in the recitation. Both printed texts give ظ.

30.2.4.head: الوِراد
30.2.4.meaning: Tawny or reddish in colour, describing the lions.

32.1.3.head: المِرّيخ
32.1.3.meaning: Mars, the planet with a distinctly reddish appearance.

33.1.4.head: سُهَيل
33.1.4.meaning: Canopus, a bright star seen in the southern sky.

35.2.3.head: ظِنَّة
35.2.3.meaning: A surmise, here what the mounts take to be the coming dawn.

35.2.4.head: زِناد
35.2.4.meaning: Fire sticks or a fire-striker, used to produce a spark.

37.2.1.head: تَعالَّ
37.2.1.meaning: Drew on the last remnant or wrung out what remained.

40.1.2.head: الرّوم
40.1.2.meaning: Byzantines, here the people who sail the Mediterranean.

41.1.3.head: السَّفين
41.1.3.meaning: Ships collectively. The t heard immediately afterwards begins the next verb.

43.1.2.head: سَفر
43.1.2.meaning: A travelling company, here the crews aboard the ships.

45.2.1.head: راوَحَ
45.2.1.meaning: Is visited or supplied in the evening.

45.2.4.head: غادى
45.2.4.meaning: Is visited or supplied in the morning.

48.2.5.head: عَتاد
48.2.5.meaning: Equipment or provisions kept ready for use.

52.1.2.head: الأَصادِق
52.1.2.meaning: Friends or trusted companions, an uncommon plural.

52.1.3.head: مُستَقيد
52.1.3.meaning: Willing to be guided, here by his friends.

53.1.4.head: كَيد
53.1.4.meaning: Working at a matter, planning it with care.

54.2.3.meaning: Came to the brink of achieving something.

55.1.2.head: التَّنَصُّح
55.1.2.meaning: Making an earnest effort to counsel someone well.

56.2.4.head: أَلا
56.2.4.meaning: Spare an effort or fall short, here with a negative.
